label: Minimal-shape cold start + hot path (default budget)
subject: samples/MinimalApp

notes.coldStartMs: Baseline 420 ms is the minimum of six Release boots of samples/MinimalApp on a QUIET 2026-09-12 dev machine (420/445/456/458/459/477). The same six boots on the SAME machine under load measured 1378/1461/1599/1645/2388/2564 - min 1378, over 3x the quiet minimum. That second run is why the ceiling is 6000 and not Phase 16's 2000: 2 s was measured once by hand on a deployment target and is a fine claim about a deployment, but as a CI ceiling on a shared runner it would flake, and a gate that flakes is a gate people disable. 6000 is ~14x the quiet baseline and ~4.4x the loaded one.
notes.hotPathMs: 5 ms against a 0.36 ms quiet baseline is deliberately ~14x slack; the loaded run measured min 0.688 ms (median 5.6 ms, which is why the gate reads min and not median). These ceilings exist to catch an ORDER-OF-MAGNITUDE regression - a default path that starts doing I/O, a middleware registered unconditionally, a per-request allocation storm - not a percent-level one. Slack that has gone stale is not left to anyone's memory: every green run prints the measured headroom ratio, and ToolUp.Platform.Build.Tests refuses a ceiling more than 20x its recorded baseline.
notes.statistic: Wallclock noise on a shared runner is one-sided - a neighbouring job can only make a boot slower - so the minimum over N runs is the least contaminated estimate, and the only statistic whose spread does not widen as the runner gets busier.
notes.absentAssemblies: The zero-cost-when-unused invariant (GP 13, and the Phase 9y 'default-on DROPPED' conclusion) made byte-level rather than timed. A companion nobody registered should not be in the deployment at all - which is checkable exactly, where 'costs no measurable time' is not.
notes.remotingDispatchColdStart: Recorded, not gated (Phase 906). Phase 804's ToolUp.Remoting.Benchmarks re-run after the generated invocation moved INSIDE the proxy: cold start of dispatching five methods of the sample's 40-method echo contract in a fresh process, min of 7 boots, Release, 16 logical cores, .NET 10.0.8, 2026-09-29, on a LOADED machine (other build-and-test sessions beside it). Generated table registered, dispatched through the proxy the adapter builds - the route a deployment takes, inside the pre-flight chain: 89.1 ms (standalone boots) / 109.8 ms (within the full report run). Reflective proxy, nothing registered: 107.7 / 122.7 ms; before the phase, the same arm on the same machine the same day measured 113.2 ms. Phase 804's direct floor - a typed call with no proxy and so no chain, which no deployment may use: 77.4 / 89.6 ms. So the safe route keeps roughly 13-18 ms (12-17 %) of the ~30 ms 804 measured for the bypass; per-request cost is level with reflection. Reproduce: dotnet build src/ToolUp.Remoting.Benchmarks -c Release, then dotnet src/ToolUp.Remoting.Benchmarks/bin/Release/net10.0/ToolUp.Remoting.Benchmarks.dll --boots 7 --rounds 9 (or --cold dispatch generated|reflection|direct for one boot).
notes.reviewing-a-change: Raising a ceiling is a claim that the SDK is now legitimately slower. Say why in this block, in the same diff.

client.label: Browser runtime under Node - boot, decode, dispatch-to-render (Phase 849); production bundle sizes (Phase 909)
client.subject: samples/MinimalClient (boot; its production build and the SDK shell's) + src/ToolUp.AI.Client.Tests ClientBench (decode over tests/remoting-corpus, dispatch over a 200-row view)

notes.remeasured: Phase 909 re-measured every clock below on Phase 884's tree, by the rule Phase 849 set them by (minimum over three production-build ClientBench runs, seed 849001, 6 boots, 9 rounds), because 884 found the seeded generator ClientBench orders its work by had overflowed under Fable - after a few draws every value was 0, so 849's baselines were taken over a near-degenerate decode order and dispatch sequence. Machine: Windows 11, Intel Core Ultra 9 386H, 16 logical processors, node v25.9.0 win32/x64, 2026-09-29. Three runs on 884's own tree while six other build-and-test sessions shared the machine (CPU 51-72%): boot 617.0 / 622.5 / 603.7 ms, decode 3.921 / 2.523 / 1.648 us, view 375.3 / 358.6 / 392.6 us. The three runs the baselines are taken from are on the tree this phase shipped (884's plus the bundle and generated-module legs, which run in child processes and do not touch the in-process decode and view loops), at 9-14% CPU for two of them. Every ceiling moved down, because every baseline did; both numbers are in each note. The two causes cannot be separated after the fact: 849's runs were taken at a load average of 100%, and 884's fix changed the order the rounds walk.
notes.bootMs: Baseline 529.77 ms (was 1265): the minimum of three production-build runs, 529.77 / 536.08 / 534.79. Ceiling 7500 ms (was 17500), ~14x, Phase 192's slack ratio - the loaded runs on 884's tree (603.7 min) sit at 12x headroom under it. Boot is import() of the transpiled samples/MinimalClient to its first commit into #elmish-app under jsdom; import cost transfers to a browser, paint does not (jsdom lays nothing out and AG Charts draws into a no-op canvas).
notes.decodePerResponseUs: Baseline 1.545 us (was 5.66): the minimum of 1.559 / 1.588 / 1.545, the proxy's 200 path - SimpleJson.parseNative then Convert.fromJsonAs over createTypeInfo - averaged across the 72 cross-host wire-corpus .json fixtures that decode to their declared value (decimal-max and date-timespan-negative do not, and are excluded by name on every run). JSON.parse alone over the same bytes measured 0.236 us and parseNative alone 0.619 us in the same runs. Ceiling 22 us (was 80), ~14x. The loaded runs on 884's tree reached 3.921 us, 5.6x headroom under it. Decode is the same JavaScript a browser runs.
notes.viewPerDispatchUs: Baseline 315.29 us (was 906): the minimum of 385.08 / 371.78 / 315.29 of the view the render hook builds per dispatched message - a 200-row Feliz table, one render-hook call per message - with React's production build (the development build is refused by the harness, it validates every element). Ceiling 4400 us (was 12500), ~14x. View construction is the same JavaScript a browser runs; React's commit and paint are not in this number.
notes.minimalBundleKiB: Baseline 2663.43 KiB = 2,727,355 bytes: the one .js file `vite build` writes for samples/MinimalClient's index.html (790,119 bytes gzipped, a lever in the measurement file). Nearly all of it is the npm dependencies the sample's view pulls in (AG Grid, React); the sample never reaches the SDK shell, the remoting proxies or the generated client module, so this number moves with the sample's own reach and its dependency pins. A SIZE, not a clock: three builds from two separate Fable compiles wrote the same file byte for byte (same content hash in its name), so there is no noise for slack to absorb. The ceiling is therefore NOT the clocks' 14x: 2730 KiB, 1.025x, about 67 KiB of growth before a reviewed raise.
notes.shellBundleKiB: Baseline 3851.92 KiB = 3,944,367 bytes: `vite build --config vite.shell.config.mts` in samples/MinimalClient - the SDK shell's module graph (SDK.Client as the entry, every export kept), which holds the remoting proxies and the Phase 853 generated client module (1,058,664 bytes gzipped). Byte-identical across three builds, like the minimal bundle. Ceiling 3950 KiB, 1.025x: about 98 KiB of headroom, which is LESS than one more generated module the size of Phase 853's (its transpiled module minifies alone to 113,152 bytes), so the next one fails this gate instead of growing the bundle unseen. Measured on Windows; if the Linux runner's build differs by more than the headroom on its first run, re-take the baseline from that run's artefact and say so here - a platform difference is not a regression.
notes.bundle-headroom: Why the two sizes do not use the clocks' ~14x: that slack exists because wallclock noise on a shared runner is one-sided, and a size has none. ToolUp.Platform.Build.Tests holds every shipped bundle ceiling to at most 1.1x its baseline, beside the 20x law every client ceiling is held to.
notes.statistic: Min over rounds (decode, view) and over fresh-process boots (boot), for Phase 192's reason: wallclock noise is one-sided.
notes.reproducing: pwsh ./dev-scripts/perf-budget-gate.ps1 -SkipServer -SkipLoad runs the whole client half: the two production builds into artifacts/perf-budget/bundles/, then, in src/ToolUp.AI.Client.Tests, NODE_ENV=production node --import ./register-loader.mjs output/Program.js ClientBench --seed 849001 --minimal-bundle <dir> --shell-bundle <dir>. The seed orders the fixtures and the dispatch sequence, and is printed beside the runtime on every run.
notes.reviewing-a-change: Raising a client ceiling is a claim that the client runtime is now legitimately slower, or its bundle legitimately larger. Say why here, in the same diff; ToolUp.Platform.Build.Tests refuses any ceiling more than 20x its baseline, and any bundle ceiling more than 1.1x.

load.label: Fact and retrieval paths under concurrent load (Phase 886)
load.subject: src/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks `load gate`: retrieval = flat store, memory blob arm, 10,000 chunks, 8 concurrent callers, 200 queries x 5 rounds; facts = BlobFactStore, memory blob arm, 1,000 subjects x 3 metrics x 4 weeks (12,000 facts), 4 concurrent callers, 20 operations x 5 rounds per operation

notes.machine: Every baseline is the minimum over three `load gate` runs on 2026-09-28: Windows 11, Intel Core Ultra 9 386H, 16 logical processors, 31.5 GB. It was NOT a quiet machine - six build-and-test sessions ran beside it, CPU load read 93% and 2.5 GB of memory was free - so, like the client block's baselines, these overstate the quiet cost. The per-run spread shows it: the population read's min-over-rounds p95 was 87.15 / 13.40 / 32.54 ms across the three runs.
notes.retrievalP95Ms: Baseline 32.38 ms (runs: 42.16 / 32.38 / 41.38). The value is the p95 of TOTAL retrieval latency within one round - measured around IRetrievalPipeline.Retrieve by RagTelemetry.RetrievalMeter, embedding, dense search, BM25, fusion and merge included - and the gate reads the minimum over five rounds. Ceiling ~14x (Phase 192's slack ratio).
notes.retrievalBlobReadsPerQuery: Baseline 0: once the scope's index is loaded (the warm-up pays it), the flat store and the BM25 index answer from memory and read no blob per query. The count is deterministic, so its ceiling is the baseline itself: a retrieval path that starts reading blobs per query has changed shape, whatever the clock says. On object storage each read is a request, which is why this is gated beside the clock rather than instead of it.
notes.factPointReadMs: Baseline 182.52 ms (runs: 297.36 / 182.52 / 268.20). A subject-and-metric read (FactQuery.forSubjectMetric, latest week) - which BlobFactStore answers by enumerating and deserialising every fact in the scope. Ceiling ~14x.
notes.factPopulationReadMs: Baseline 13.40 ms (runs: 87.15 / 13.40 / 32.54 - the widest spread in the block, and the reason its ceiling is ~13x of the quiet-est run rather than of the median). A top-10 population read over one metric's latest week; the scope is above the Phase 702 surface's 512-head threshold, so the surface is consulted (491 blob reads per read on average, cold builds included, against 12,000 for the enumerating point read). Ceiling ~13x.
notes.factAssertMs: Baseline 243.71 ms (runs: 252.64 / 243.71 / 347.36). One Assert superseding the latest week of a distinct subject - which reads every fact in scope to find the lineage head. Ceiling ~14x.
notes.factBatchAssertMs: Baseline 233.38 ms (runs: 312.27 / 233.38 / 301.97). One AssertBatch of 50 drafts, each superseding. Ceiling ~14x.
notes.factBlobReadsPerPointRead: Baseline 12,000 = every fact in the 12,000-fact scope: the point read is O(store), and this count is what says so on any backend. Deterministic, so the ceiling is 1.5x rather than an order of magnitude: reading the scope twice per read is a regression the clock might hide on a busy runner and the count cannot.
notes.statistic: Min over rounds, for Phase 192's reason: wallclock noise is one-sided. Each round is a closed loop of N concurrent callers; a round's value is the p95 of its own operations.
notes.reproducing: dotnet build src/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks -c Release, then dotnet src/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks/bin/Release/net10.0/ToolUp.RAG.Benchmarks.dll load gate --measurements artifacts/perf-budget/load-measurements.json. The full matrix (other stores, blob arms and sizes) is `load retrieval` / `load facts`; docs/rag/performance.md records what it measured.
notes.reviewing-a-change: Raising a load ceiling is a claim that the fact or retrieval path is now legitimately slower. Say why here, in the same diff; ToolUp.Platform.Build.Tests refuses any ceiling more than 20x its baseline.
